key: Purity and stillness give the correct law to all under heaven.
s: Ending a chapter where great things seem their opposites, the verse makes stillness the rule; Wang Bi, on chapter 45, reads stillness as keeping whole the truth of things and agitation as violating their nature, so only purity and stillness reach the chapter’s great things.
src: Wang Bi, Laozi zhu, chapter 45, zh.wikisource (the Huating Zhang edition), revision 2354026 (2024)

evidence.words: 靜則全物之真，躁則犯物之性，故惟清靜，乃得如上諸大也。
evidence.gloss: Stillness keeps whole the truth of things; agitation violates the nature of things. So only through purity and stillness are all the great things above attained.

reason: Both problems hold. Plain sense now says what the verse does (it makes stillness the rule, from 清靜為天下正, with no four-word run from Legge’s line), and the reading ends on “the chapter’s great things”, anchored in the plain sense’s “great things seem their opposites”, instead of “named above”. Re-opened packet.js tao 45: Wang Bi on 躁勝寒，靜勝熱。清靜為天下正 writes 靜則全物之真，躁則犯物之性，故惟清靜，乃得如上諸大也, and 如上諸大 are the chapter’s great completion, fullness, straightness, skill and eloquence. The critic’s wording measured 46, so “draws a rule from stillness” became “makes stillness the rule”. verse.js ok (Tao Te Ching 45, at [44]); entry-check ok, 45 words.
